FIXED + VERIFIED 2026-07-16 (commit 8311cdb; thomas confirmed the render in a browser). DECK_BASE_URL is now the https REST endpoint https://cbc-wilm-agent-public.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. The emailed link is https:// and opens clean — no interstitial is possible on https by construction, and the deck renders correctly. This closed for a much better reason than the one it was filed with. The original decision was "accept http, it is only a cosmetic interstitial". That was WRONG: http did not merely look bad, it BROKE the deck. The origin is baked into every at render time, so an http origin served over https had all 37 backgrounds blocked as insecure mixed content — perfect text and layout, zero images, no error. Found by thomas opening the real URL after curl-based checks had pronounced it fine. https turned out strictly better rather than merely nicer: mixed-content blocking only applies to insecure subresources on a SECURE page, never the reverse, so https images render from BOTH the REST and website endpoints, while http images render from only one. Option (1) was taken and the website configuration was KEPT — contrary to the original design note, dropping it was unnecessary, since nothing depends on its index-document suffix (decks are always explicit .../index.html paths). ROOT CAUSE: infra/outputs.tf described the website endpoint as "use as the media asset base for build-deck.js". The wrong thing was the documented thing. Now emits deck_rest_endpoint as the one to use (outputs-only; needs a terraform apply to refresh). PINNED: agent/tests/test_publish.py asserts the default origin is https and never an s3-website host, and that the asset base and deck link share one origin. FUTURE: a CloudFront + custom domain front (the original option 2) remains available whenever wanted. The date-keyed path scheme survives it, so links already emailed keep working.

ACCEPTANCE FULLY MET 2026-07-16 (thomas verified BOTH cases in a real browser). Commits: bucket CORS in bs-crp/infra/s3.tf, crossorigin emission in 32a9aeb. - JPEG export from the HOSTED S3 URL: no SecurityError. - JPEG export from a LOCALLY rendered preview pointed at the S3 asset base (/tmp/local-preview-s3/service-preview.html, built with --asset-base https://cbc-wilm-agent-public.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/templates/service): no SecurityError. THIS is the case the issue exists for — a file:// page pulling images genuinely cross-origin — and it passing is what actually proves both halves work together: S3 returns ACAO (verified on the wire: ACAO * on a cross-origin GET) AND the elements opt in with crossorigin="anonymous", so the canvas is never tainted. WHY BOTH CASES WERE NEEDED, worth keeping. The hosted pass alone proves almost nothing about tainting: DECK_BASE_URL is the bucket's own origin, so a deck served from the bucket loads its templates SAME-ORIGIN and the browser never consults CORS at all — same-origin passes first. The hosted test only shows crossorigin="anonymous" does not BREAK the same-origin path. The local-preview test is the one that exercises the actual mechanism. Anyone re-verifying this after a change must run the local case; a green hosted export is not evidence. BOTH HALVES REMAIN REQUIRED. CORS response headers alone do not untaint a canvas — without crossorigin="anonymous" the browser never sends Origin and S3's ACAO goes unused. And the attribute alone does nothing without the bucket returning ACAO. Removing either one reintroduces the bug, and it fails CONFUSINGLY: the slides still render correctly and only Export throws.

THE ONE THAT NEARLY SHIPPED BROKEN — read before touching DECK_BASE_URL. The first published deck used the http website endpoint as its origin. This tool bakes that origin into every AT RENDER TIME, so opening the deck over https made the browser block all 37 backgrounds as insecure mixed content: perfect text, perfect layout, no images, NO ERROR ANYWHERE. It survived a full round of curl-based verification because every object returned 200 individually — and 200-per-object does not imply the page renders. Caught only when a human opened the URL. Fixed via bs-a4a (https REST endpoint) and pinned by tests asserting the origin is https and never an s3-website host. LESSON FOR RE-VERIFYING THIS: status codes are not evidence of rendering.
